description: Recipes for solving problems and the science of how costly they are: complexity, sorting, searching, recursion, dynamic programming, greedy methods, graph algorithms, backtracking, randomness, and the limits of what can be computed. The `algorithms` concept itself lives in mathematics.json.

concepts.title: Big O
concepts.summary: How the cost of an algorithm grows as its input grows, ignoring constants. Doubling the input might double the work, quadruple it, or barely change it, and that pattern matters far more than the speed of any one machine.

concepts.title: Time Complexity
concepts.summary: How the number of steps an algorithm takes grows with the size of its input. Constant, logarithmic, linear, quadratic, exponential: each class is a different world, and the gaps between them widen fast.

concepts.title: Space Complexity
concepts.summary: How much extra memory an algorithm needs as its input grows. Speed and memory often trade off: a lookup table makes things fast by remembering, and a frugal method may recompute instead.

concepts.title: Amortized Analysis
concepts.summary: Averaging the cost over a whole sequence of operations rather than per operation. A dynamic array's append is occasionally very costly, but spread across many appends the cost is constant, and this makes that precise.

concepts.title: Best and Worst Case
concepts.summary: The same algorithm can be quick on friendly input and slow on hostile input. Worst case gives a guarantee, best case is rarely useful, and average case says what to expect if the input is typical.

concepts.title: P versus NP
concepts.summary: Can every problem whose answer is easy to check also be solved easily? Most experts think not, but nobody has proved it, and a proof either way would reshape computing, cryptography, and mathematics. It carries a million-dollar prize.

concepts.title: NP-Completeness
concepts.summary: The hardest problems among those whose answers can be quickly checked. If a fast method existed for any one of them, it would give a fast method for all. Thousands of practical problems have been shown to be in this club.

concepts.title: Travelling Salesman
concepts.summary: Find the shortest route that visits every city once and returns. Easy to state, and the number of routes explodes as cities are added, so exact solutions are out of reach for large inputs and clever approximations do the work.

concepts.title: Sorting
concepts.summary: Putting things in order. It is among the most studied problems in computing because so much else depends on it: searching, merging, removing duplicates. Dozens of methods exist, and each is a lesson in trade-offs between speed, memory, and stability.

concepts.title: Bubble Sort
concepts.summary: Repeatedly step through the list, swapping neighbors that are out of order, until nothing moves. Easy to grasp and slow on large inputs, taking time proportional to the square of the length, so it is mostly used for teaching.

concepts.title: Insertion Sort
concepts.summary: Build a sorted list one item at a time by sliding each new item back to its place, like sorting playing cards in your hand. Slow for large random input, fast on nearly sorted data, and used for small pieces inside faster sorts.

concepts.title: Selection Sort
concepts.summary: Find the smallest remaining item, put it next, and repeat. It makes very few swaps but always scans everything, so it takes square time even on sorted input. Simple and predictable, and rarely the best choice.

concepts.title: Merge Sort
concepts.summary: Split the list in half, sort each half, and merge them. It always takes n log n steps and keeps equal items in their original order, at the cost of extra memory. A textbook case of divide and conquer, and good for data on disk.

concepts.title: Quicksort
concepts.summary: Pick a pivot, put smaller items to its left and larger to its right, and repeat on each side. Usually the fastest in practice despite a quadratic worst case, which is why pivot choice and randomization get so much care.

concepts.title: Heapsort
concepts.summary: Build a heap from the data, then repeatedly take the largest off the top. Guaranteed n log n time and almost no extra memory, though it jumps around memory, so it is often slower in practice than quicksort.

concepts.title: Counting Sort
concepts.summary: Sort whole numbers in a small range by counting how many times each appears, then writing them out in order. It never compares items, so it beats the n log n limit for comparison sorts when the range is small.

concepts.title: Radix Sort
concepts.summary: Sort numbers or words digit by digit, from the last to the first, using a stable pass at each step. It also avoids comparisons, and is used on large sets of integers, dates, and fixed-length keys.

concepts.title: Timsort
concepts.summary: A hybrid sort that finds runs already in order and merges them, using insertion sort on small pieces. Designed for real-world data, which is often partly sorted, and the standard sort in Python, Java, and Android.

concepts.title: Searching
concepts.summary: Finding an item in a collection, or deciding it is not there. How fast you can do it depends on what you know about the collection: unordered data forces a full scan, while order or hashing lets you skip almost everything.

concepts.title: Linear Search
concepts.summary: Look at every item in turn until you find the one you want. It works on anything, and is the best you can do when nothing is known about the order. It takes time proportional to the size of the collection.

concepts.title: Binary Search
concepts.summary: In a sorted list, look at the middle and discard the half that cannot contain the answer, then repeat. A million items take about twenty steps. The idea is simple and famously easy to get subtly wrong.

concepts.title: Interpolation Search
concepts.summary: Like binary search, but guess where the item should be from its value, the way you open a phone book near the end for a name starting with W. Fast on evenly spread data, slow on lumpy data.

concepts.title: String Search
concepts.summary: Finding a short pattern inside a long text. Checking every position is slow; clever methods use what a failed match already revealed to skip ahead. It is behind find in every editor and much of bioinformatics.

concepts.title: Knuth–Morris–Pratt
concepts.summary: A string search that never re-reads text. On a mismatch, it uses a precomputed table of the pattern's own repeats to jump ahead. It takes time proportional to the text plus the pattern length.

concepts.title: Regular Expressions
concepts.summary: A compact notation for describing patterns in text: letters, choices, repeats. Behind it, a pattern can be turned into a state machine that reads the text once. Powerful, famously hard to read, and easy to make slow.

concepts.title: Recursion
concepts.summary: A definition or a procedure that refers to itself on a smaller version of the problem. Reduce until you hit something trivial, then build back up. It fits things with self-similar shape, such as trees and fractals.

concepts.title: Divide and Conquer
concepts.summary: Split a problem into smaller copies of itself, solve each, and combine the answers. Merge sort, quicksort, binary search, and fast multiplication all work this way, and the gains come from the halving.

concepts.title: Tail Calls
concepts.summary: A function call that is the very last thing a function does, so the old frame is no longer needed. Languages that optimize it can turn deep recursion into a loop with no growing stack.

concepts.title: Recurrences
concepts.summary: An equation that defines each term from earlier ones, such as F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2). It is how the running time of a recursive algorithm is written down, and solving it turns a recursive structure into a closed-form cost.

concepts.title: Master Theorem
concepts.summary: A shortcut for solving the running time of divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n). It compares the work at the top with the work at the bottom and tells you which one dominates.

concepts.title: Fibonacci
concepts.summary: Each number is the sum of the two before: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. The simple recursive version repeats work so wildly that it takes exponential time, which makes it the standard example of why remembering answers matters.

concepts.title: Dynamic Programming
concepts.summary: Solve a big problem by solving overlapping smaller ones once each and remembering the answers. When a problem repeats its own subproblems, this turns exponential recursion into a table fill of manageable size.

concepts.title: Memoization
concepts.summary: Save the result of a call and reuse it when the same inputs come up again. It turns a slow recursion with repeated work into a fast one at the cost of memory, and is the top-down way of writing dynamic programming.

concepts.title: Optimal Substructure
concepts.summary: A problem has it when the best solution is built from best solutions of its parts. If so, dynamic programming or greedy methods may work. If not, a locally best choice can hide the globally best answer.

concepts.title: Knapsack Problem
concepts.summary: You can carry only so much; each item has a weight and a value; choose what to take. Trying every combination is exponential, yet a table over the capacity solves it quickly for reasonable numbers. It models budgeting and packing everywhere.

concepts.title: Common Subsequence
concepts.summary: Find the longest sequence of items that appears in both inputs in order, though not necessarily side by side. It is the core of diff tools and of comparing DNA sequences, and a standard dynamic programming table.

concepts.title: Edit Distance
concepts.summary: The minimum number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to turn one string into another. It measures how alike two words are, and drives spell-checking, fuzzy search, and DNA alignment.

concepts.title: Greedy Algorithms
concepts.summary: At each step take the choice that looks best right now and never look back. It is fast and simple, and it works exactly when the problem has the right structure; otherwise a locally best step can lead you astray.

concepts.title: Huffman Coding
concepts.summary: Give common symbols short codes and rare ones long codes, built greedily by merging the two rarest each time. It produces the best possible prefix code and is a stage inside ZIP, JPEG, and MP3.

concepts.title: Making Change
concepts.summary: Pay an amount with the fewest coins. Taking the biggest coin first is optimal for many coin systems but not all: with coins of 1, 3, and 4, making 6 greedily gives 4+1+1 rather than 3+3.

concepts.title: Spanning Trees
concepts.summary: Connect all the nodes of a network using the least total edge cost and no loops. It is the cheapest way to wire towns or lay a network, and greedy algorithms find it exactly.

concepts.title: Kruskal's Algorithm
concepts.summary: Sort the edges by cost and add each one unless it would close a loop, using union-find to check. It ends with a minimum spanning tree, built as a forest of pieces that gradually merge.

concepts.title: Prim's Algorithm
concepts.summary: Grow a tree from one node, always adding the cheapest edge that reaches a new node. Like Kruskal's, it finds a minimum spanning tree, and with a priority queue it works well on dense graphs.

concepts.title: Interval Scheduling
concepts.summary: Pick the most non-overlapping jobs from a list of time slots. Always choosing the one that finishes earliest is provably best, and it is the neatest proof that a greedy rule can be exactly right.

concepts.title: Graph Algorithms
concepts.summary: Ways to explore and measure a network: visiting every node, finding shortest routes, ordering dependencies, spreading flow. Since so much is a graph, these are among the most widely reused algorithms in computing.

concepts.title: Breadth-First Search
concepts.summary: Explore a graph in rings: all neighbors first, then their neighbors, and so on, using a queue. It finds the fewest-step path in an unweighted graph, and underlies web crawlers and friend-of-friend searches.

concepts.title: Depth-First Search
concepts.summary: Go as deep as you can down one path, then back up and try the next, using a stack or recursion. It finds cycles, orders dependencies, and solves mazes, and uses little memory.

concepts.title: Shortest Paths
concepts.summary: Finding the cheapest route between nodes in a weighted graph: fastest roads, fewest network hops, lowest cost. Which algorithm to use depends on whether weights can be negative and whether you want one route or all of them.

concepts.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.summary: Always extend the closest unvisited node, using a priority queue, and the cheapest route to every node is settled in order. Fast and correct when no edge has negative cost; it is inside GPS routing and network protocols such as OSPF.

concepts.title: Bellman–Ford
concepts.summary: Shortest paths that tolerate negative edge costs by relaxing every edge again and again. Slower than Dijkstra, but it can also detect a negative cycle, and it inspired distance-vector routing in networks.

concepts.title: Floyd–Warshall
concepts.summary: Shortest paths between every pair of nodes, computed by asking, for each node in turn, whether going through it improves any route. A tidy dynamic programming triple loop that takes cubic time.

concepts.title: A* Search
concepts.summary: Dijkstra with a sense of direction: it prefers nodes that look closer to the goal, using an estimate. If the estimate never overshoots, the answer is still the best. Widely used in games, robots, and maps.

concepts.title: Topological Sort
concepts.summary: Put the nodes of a directed acyclic graph in an order where every arrow points forward. It tells you a valid order for building, installing, or taking courses, and fails only if there is a cycle.

concepts.title: Maximum Flow
concepts.summary: How much can flow from a source to a sink through a network whose pipes have limits? The maximum equals the capacity of the smallest cut separating them, and the result solves matching, scheduling, and traffic problems.

concepts.title: PageRank
concepts.summary: Rank pages by the chance that someone following links at random would land on them. Links from important pages count more, an idea that turned the web's graph into the basis of early Google search.

concepts.title: Connected Components
concepts.summary: The separate islands of a graph, where every node can reach every other within its own island. Finding them tells you whether a network is one piece, and how many parts it splits into.

concepts.title: Backtracking
concepts.summary: Build a solution step by step, and whenever a partial one cannot possibly work, undo the last step and try another. It searches an enormous space while cutting off branches that are already doomed.

concepts.title: Eight Queens
concepts.summary: Place eight chess queens on a board so that none attacks another. Trying every arrangement is huge, but backtracking abandons a board the moment two queens clash, and the puzzle has 92 solutions.

concepts.title: Solving Sudoku
concepts.summary: Solving Sudoku by machine: fill a cell, check the rules, and back up when stuck, with smart ordering of which cell to try first. A tidy example of constraints narrowing a search.

concepts.title: Constraint Solving
concepts.summary: Problems described as variables, possible values, and rules between them: timetables, puzzles, configuration. Solvers propagate what each choice rules out, which prunes the search far more than blind trial.

concepts.title: Branch and Bound
concepts.summary: Search a tree of choices while tracking the best answer so far, and prune any branch whose best possible outcome is already worse. It solves hard optimization problems, such as scheduling, exactly.

concepts.title: Minimax
concepts.summary: In a two-player game, assume your opponent plays the best reply and choose the move that leaves you best off. Searching that game tree, with pruning, is how classic chess programs decided.

concepts.title: Randomized Algorithms
concepts.summary: Algorithms that flip coins to decide what to do. Randomness protects against bad inputs, simplifies design, and sometimes makes otherwise slow problems fast, at the price of an answer that is only right with high probability.

concepts.title: Monte Carlo
concepts.summary: Estimate something by running many random trials and averaging. Throw random points at a square with a circle in it and the hit rate approximates pi. Used where exact calculation is out of reach, from physics to finance.

concepts.title: Las Vegas Algorithms
concepts.summary: A randomized algorithm that is always correct but whose running time varies with the luck of the coin flips. Randomized quicksort is the standard example. It contrasts with Monte Carlo methods, which are fast but sometimes wrong.

concepts.title: Simulated Annealing
concepts.summary: Search for a good solution by allowing some worse moves early, when 'hot', and fewer as it 'cools'. Borrowed from how metal is annealed, it escapes local dead ends and works on hard layout and routing problems.

concepts.title: Genetic Algorithms
concepts.summary: Evolve solutions: keep a population, favor those that score well, combine and mutate them, repeat. It borrows selection from biology, and is useful when a problem has a rugged landscape and no clean method.

concepts.title: Computability
concepts.summary: What can be computed at all, whatever the time and memory. Some well-defined questions have no algorithm that answers them in every case, and this field maps where that boundary lies.

concepts.title: Turing Machines
concepts.summary: An idealized machine: a tape, a head that reads and writes symbols, and a small table of rules. Simple as it is, anything a computer can compute can be computed by one, which made it the standard definition of an algorithm.

concepts.title: The Halting Problem
concepts.summary: Can a program decide, for any program and input, whether it will eventually stop? Turing proved it cannot. It is the first and most famous problem no algorithm can solve, and a cousin of Gödel's incompleteness.

concepts.title: Church–Turing Thesis
concepts.summary: The claim that anything effectively computable by a mechanical procedure can be computed by a Turing machine. It cannot be proved, since 'effective' is informal, but every model proposed so far has turned out equivalent.

concepts.title: Lambda Calculus
concepts.summary: A minimal language of pure functions: nothing but naming an input and applying one function to another. Church built it in the 1930s as a rival to Turing machines, and it became the seed of functional programming.

concepts.title: State Machines
concepts.summary: A system that is always in one of a few states and moves between them on inputs: a traffic light, a vending machine, a protocol. Simple to draw and to check, and the basis of pattern matching, parsers, and network handshakes.
